title: Strict integral birational law on Chevalley root coordinates
statement:
Let $\mathcal R=(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a finite reduced root datum and $(G,T_{\mathbf Q}=D_{\mathbf Q}(M))$ a split realization over $\mathbf Q$, with base and pinning forgotten, in the sense of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Assume that $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf Z\Phi^\vee=M^\vee$. There exist a base $\Delta$, orderings of its positive and negative roots, and rational root-subgroup isomorphisms $p_\alpha:\mathbf G_{a,\mathbf Q}\simeq U_\alpha\subset G$ with the following properties. Put $T_{\mathbf Z}=D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group] and
$$C=\left(\prod_{\alpha\in-\Phi^+}\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf Z}\right)\times T_{\mathbf Z}\times\left(\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf Z}\right).$$
Here $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$, $\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf Z}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z[z]$, and $D_R(M)=\operatorname{Spec}R[M]$. This is a smooth separated scheme of finite presentation over $\mathbf Z$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], with nonempty geometrically integral fibres. Separated means that its diagonal is a closed immersion. The coordinate maps $q_\alpha:\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf Z}\to C$ set all other additive coordinates to zero and the torus coordinate to $1$; $q_T:T_{\mathbf Z}\to C$ sets all additive coordinates to zero. Write $e=(0,1,0)$. The map
$$c:C_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow G,\qquad (a,t,b)\longmapsto\left(\prod p_\alpha(a_\alpha)\right)t\left(\prod p_\alpha(b_\alpha)\right)$$
is an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion] with geometrically dense image, carries $q_{\alpha,\mathbf Q}$ to $p_\alpha$ and $q_{T,\mathbf Q}$ to the specified torus, and carries $e$ to $1$.

There are opens $V\subset C\times_{\mathbf Z}C$ [def-pc-fibre-product] and $J\subset C$ and morphisms $m:V\to C$, $\iota:J\to C$ extending the multiplication and inversion induced by $c$ on the generic fibre. The opens are dense in every fibre over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$; $V$ contains $C\times\{e\}$, $\{e\}\times C$, $q_T(T_{\mathbf Z})^2$ and $q_\alpha(\mathbf A^1)^2$ for every root, and $J$ contains the torus and all the root axes. On these subgroup squares $m$ is respectively the monomial torus law and addition; $e$ is a two-sided identity. The rational map $m:C\times C\dashrightarrow C$ is associative as a rational map, has rational inverse $\iota$, and is strict in the following precise sense. There is an open $D\subset V$ such that
$$ (x,y)\longmapsto(x,m(x,y)),\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto(m(x,y),y) $$
are open immersions of $D$ into $C\times C$, and $D$ and both images are dense in every fibre of each projection $C\times C\to C$. A rational map here means a morphism on a fibrewise dense open, modulo agreement on a fibrewise dense common open.

These same parameters $p_\alpha$, used in $c$, satisfy the following morphism identities over $\mathbf Q$ for every root $\alpha$:
$$t p_\alpha(z)t^{-1}=p_\alpha(\chi_\alpha(t)z),$$
$$p_\alpha(u)p_{-\alpha}(v)=p_{-\alpha}\left(\frac v{1+uv}\right)\alpha^\vee(1+uv)p_\alpha\left(\frac u{1+uv}\right)\quad\text{on }D(1+uv),$$
and, with $w_\alpha=p_\alpha(1)p_{-\alpha}(-1)p_\alpha(1)$,
$$w_\alpha p_\alpha(z)w_\alpha^{-1}=p_{-\alpha}(-z).$$
Here $\chi_\alpha(t)=t(e^\alpha)$ and $\alpha^\vee$ is the prescribed monomial cocharacter. The zero root datum is included. This assertion concerns only a partial law on the explicit scheme $C$; it asserts no group scheme containing $C$.

source.place: Section 6.3, Proposition 6.3.4 and the opposite-root normalization after Remark 6.3.5, Lemmas 6.3.7--6.3.9, Proposition 6.3.11, Proposition 6.3.13, printed pp.215--226; rational rank-one identities in Theorem 4.2.6(1), equation (4.2.1), and Corollary 5.1.9(3). The partial root-cell law, before adjoining translates or forming its group envelope. Read online; local PDF WANTED. No Stacks tag states this input.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality] to the given rational realization. Keep its base, parameters, orderings, groups $E_\pm$ and torus actions. The hypotheses are precisely semisimplicity and the coroot-lattice condition in the statement. The positive system $\Phi^+$ of $\Delta$ is the positive set of an integer linear functional nonzero on $\Phi$: since $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, $\Delta$ is a rational basis of it; take the rational functional equal to $1$ on every $\delta\in\Delta$ and multiply it by a common denominator of its values on a basis of $M$; every root is a sign-coherent integer combination of $\Delta$, so its sign is the sign of the functional. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-root-product-open-cell] with $A=\mathbf Q$, this functional and this $\Phi^+$ (its root subgroups $U_\alpha$ are attached to the roots, not to the functional), to get the open immersion $c:E_{-,\mathbf Q}\times T_{\mathbf Q}\times E_{+,\mathbf Q}\to G$. The root subgroups agree with those of the chosen parameters by [lem-sfb-relative-canonical-root-exponential]; their parametrizations differ only by nonzero rational scalars, which are automorphisms of the affine-line factors. Hence the same open-cell assertion holds for these parameters. Each coordinate axis and the torus inclusion has the claimed image by the displayed product formula. The image is geometrically dense: after any algebraically closed extension it is a nonempty open in the connected smooth reductive group, which is integral by [lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality] applied over that algebraically closed field (geometric connectedness is part of reductivity).

source.place: Lemmas 6.3.6--6.3.7 and equation (6.3.2), pp.217--220; Theorem 5.1.13 for the rational open cell.

proof.text: Choose a basis of the free lattice $M$, of rank $r$, and put $N=|\Phi^+|$. The coordinate ring of $C$ is $\mathbf Z[a_1,\ldots,a_N,t_1,t_1^{-1},\ldots,t_r,t_r^{-1},b_1,\ldots,b_N]$. Thus $C$ is the principal open $D(t_1\cdots t_r)$ in $\mathbf A^{2N+r}_{\mathbf Z}$. By [sbc-lem-affine-space-smooth], [lem-weil-pbc-open-immersion-etale] and [lem-sbc-smooth-relative-dimension-permanence] it is smooth, with the asserted finite presentation (the presentation adjoins inverses with equations $t_i s_i=1$). It is separated: multiplication $B\otimes_{\mathbf Z}B\to B$ is surjective, so the affine diagonal is a closed immersion. Each geometric fibre has the same Laurent-polynomial coordinate description over a field; it is a nonzero domain. Hence those fibres are nonempty and integral. The ring and all its open local rings are normal: $\mathbf Z$ is integrally closed by the coprime-numerator/denominator test for a monic equation; apply [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-normal-domain] repeatedly and [lem-weil-pbc-localization-normal-domain]. The same applies to $C\times C$. These schemes are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian].

source.place: The explicit product scheme preceding Lemma 6.3.8, p.220; elementary coordinate-ring verification, with standard affine-space and normality inputs.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-integral-longest-weyl-partial-conjugation]. Write $a=f|_{E_+}:E_+\to E_-$ and $b=f|_{E_-}:E_-\to E_+$. The map $j:E_+\times E_-\to C$, $(u,v)\mapsto(a(u),1,b(v))$, represents $\operatorname{Ad}(n)(uv)$ on the generic fibre. Set $K=j^{-1}(W')$ and $F=g\circ j:K\to C$. Then $F$ represents $uv$ in $c$-coordinates. The open $K$ contains $E_+\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times E_-$ because $W'$ contains both one-sign groups. Moreover $F(u,0)=(0,1,u)$ and $F(0,v)=(v,1,0)$, by the inverse restrictions in the cited node. Write $F=(A,h,B)$. These are actual morphisms over $\mathbf Z$; no denominators have been cleared and no integral envelope has been used.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9 and the construction needed for Proposition 6.3.11, pp.222--224; explicit opposite-sign collection through the inverse conjugation chart.

proof.text:
For $x=(a,t,b)$ and $y=(a',t',b')$, let $V$ be the inverse image of $K$ under $(x,y)\mapsto(b,a')$. If $F(b,a')=(A,h,B)$, define
$$m(x,y)=\bigl(a\cdot(t\cdot A),\ t h t',\ (t'^{-1}\cdot B)\cdot b'\bigr).$$
Dots within $E_-$ or $E_+$ are their integral group laws, and $t\cdot A$, $t'^{-1}\cdot B$ are their torus actions. These are morphisms by [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality]. Over $\mathbf Q$ the formula is $a t(AhB)t'b'=xy$. The two axis identities for $F$ show directly that $V$ contains both identity strips, $E_\pm^2$ and $T_{\mathbf Z}^2$, and that their laws are the corresponding group laws. In particular $m(x,e)=x=m(e,x)$; all root axes are additive subgroups. Every fibre of $V$ is a nonempty open of the integral fibre of $C^2$, since it contains $(e,e)$, so it is dense.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.11, pp.223--224; explicit assembly formula from opposite-sign collection.

proof.text:
Define $J$ by $(b^{-1},t^{-1}\cdot a^{-1})\in K$ for $x=(a,t,b)$. Write $F(b^{-1},t^{-1}\cdot a^{-1})=(A,h,B)$ and set
$$\iota(x)=\bigl(A,h t^{-1},t\cdot B\bigr).$$
This is a morphism on an open: the one-sign inverses and torus actions are morphisms by [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality]. On the generic fibre it equals $b^{-1}t^{-1}a^{-1}$, since this word is $F(b^{-1},t^{-1}a^{-1}t)t^{-1}$. The axis identities for $F$ imply that $J$ contains $E_-$, $E_+$ and the torus, and the formula restricts to their inverses. In particular $e\in J$ in every fibre, so $J$ is fibrewise dense. All restrictions demanded for $V$ and $J$ in the statement now follow from the subgroup-square containments already checked.

Whenever morphisms between the constructed open schemes agree over $\mathbf Q$, they agree over $\mathbf Z$ by [lemma-nagata-ext-scheme-theoretically-dominant-separated]. Indeed their domains are opens of Laurent-polynomial schemes, whose rings inject into their rationalizations on every affine open, so their generic fibres are scheme-theoretically dense. In particular left multiplication by $E_-$ and right multiplication by $E_+$ are global automorphisms of $C$, and left or right multiplication by the torus is also a global automorphism: in the formula for $m$ one collection variable is zero, and the remaining operations are one-sign translations and the torus action. Their inverses use the inverse subgroup element. Partial multiplication by two elements of the same one-sign group agrees with its actual group law. These statements also hold with the subgroup element variable, hence after every geometric base change. They justify the translation calculation in the next step without assuming that $C$ already lies in an integral group.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.11, generic-fibre identity argument, and preparation for Proposition 6.3.13, pp.224--226.

proof.text: Fix a geometric fibre and $h\in E_+$. The partial maps $L_h$ and $L_{h^{-1}}$ are defined respectively near $e$ and $h$, since $V$ contains the identity strips and $E_+^2$. Their composites are identity maps on smaller such neighbourhoods: the corresponding identity with variable $h$ is an equality over $\mathbf Q$ on its open domain and hence over $\mathbf Z$ by [lemma-nagata-ext-scheme-theoretically-dominant-separated]. Thus $dL_h|_e$ is invertible. For any $x=(a,t,b)$, $L_x=L_a L_t L_b$ near $e$ by the same variable-parameter equality. The first two maps are the global automorphisms of Step 6; hence $dL_x|_e$ is invertible. On the right, $R_a$ is locally invertible near $e$ using $E_-^2$, while $R_t,R_b$ are global automorphisms; $R_x=R_b R_t R_a$ gives invertibility of $dR_x|_e$. For $\Phi(x,y)=(x,m(x,y))$, the tangent matrix at $(x,e)$ is block triangular with diagonal $(1,dL_x|_e)$, and at $(e,x)$ its diagonal is $(1,1)$ from $m(e,y)=y$. The analogous matrices for $\Psi(x,y)=(m(x,y),y)$ are invertible by the right-translation calculation. By [lem-sfb-smooth-cotangent-etale-criterion], both maps are etale on an open $D\subset V$ containing the two identity strips: the determinant is a unit at all these geometric points, and invertibility of the finite-free differential matrix is open. Source and target are smooth by Step 2.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.13, p.226; explicit local-translation justification of the tangent calculation.

proof.text: On the generic fibre $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are open immersions, as restrictions of the automorphisms $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$ and $(x,y)\mapsto(xy,y)$ of $G^2$. Thus both maps on $D$ are birational. They are separated and of finite type (their schemes are separated Noetherian schemes of finite type over $\mathbf Z$). They are quasi-finite by the affine etale criterion [lem-weil-pbc-etale-ring-map-quasi-finite]. Apply [pqf-lem-normalization-open]. Its relative normalization is the target itself: by [lem-weil-pbc-relative-normalization], on a target affine $\operatorname{Spec}A$ its coordinate algebra is the integral closure of $A$ in the sections of the inverse image. Since the source is integral and birational, these sections embed in $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, and $A$ is integrally closed by Step 2. The closure is therefore exactly $A$. Consequently both maps $D\to C^2$ are open immersions. The affine-diagonal argument used in Step 2 gives separatedness of these morphisms as well.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.13, p.226; Zariski Main argument via Stacks Tag 02LR, lemma-quasi-finite-separated-quasi-affine (relative normalization open immersion).

proof.text: The open $D$ meets every geometric fibre of both projections by its two identity strips. Its $\Phi$-image contains the diagonal and $\{e\}\times C$; its $\Psi$-image contains the diagonal and $C\times\{e\}$. Each image therefore meets every fibre of each projection. Those fibres are geometrically integral, so these nonempty opens are dense, giving exactly the stated strictness. This also ensures the dominance needed to compose the rational multiplication maps. Associativity follows by [lemma-nagata-ext-scheme-theoretically-dominant-separated] on the common domain of the two composites, since it holds in $G$ over $\mathbf Q$; that domain contains $(e,e,e)$ in every fibre and is therefore fibrewise dense. The two inverse identities follow in the same way on the open domains of $m(x,\iota(x))$ and $m(\iota(x),x)$, which contain $e$ in every fibre. The three rational rank-one identities are precisely those of the parameters retained from [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality], including torus equivariance. For the zero root datum the assumptions force $M=0$; the rational open cell is the identity point and all constructions above are the unique maps on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$.

source.place: Propositions 6.3.11 and 6.3.13, pp.224--226; density, rational identities and the empty-root boundary case.
